project.name: Customer Portal
project.summary: A responsive web portal for a regional industrial-supplies distributor's roughly 400 business customers (1,500 users at launch, a few thousand orders a month). Each customer company has its own account, with company admins who invite colleagues as buyers, approvers or viewers; orders above a company-set limit need an approver. Customers see and search their order history, reorder a past order in one click at current prices and stock, and pay one or several open invoices by card through Stripe. Customers, products and prices, invoices and payments sync both ways with the distributor's QuickBooks Online company, with conflicts flagged to staff. Staff get a back office for companies, users, orders, payments and the sync log. New TypeScript, React, Node and Postgres codebase on a mainstream cloud.

requirements.text: Customer company accounts: each customer company has its own account; a company admin invites colleagues and assigns each a role (buyer, approver, viewer); users see only their own company's data.
Order approval: orders above a limit set by the company admin need approval from an approver before they are placed.
Order history: customers see past orders and order lines, and search and filter them.
Ordering and one-click reorder: buyers place orders; a past order can be reordered in one click at current prices and stock, and the cart shows what changed.
Invoices and card payment: customers see open invoices and pay one or several by card through Stripe; payment status updates from Stripe webhooks; card data never touches the portal's servers.

Two-way QuickBooks Online sync of customers, products and prices, invoices and payments: portal orders become QuickBooks invoices; invoices and payments recorded in QuickBooks appear in the portal; conflicts are flagged for staff, never overwritten silently.
Staff back office: manage customer companies and users, see and edit orders, see payments, see the sync log and resolve sync conflicts.
Responsive web app for desktop and phone browsers; no native mobile app.

Non-functional: about 400 companies and 1,500 users at launch, a few thousand orders a month; business contact data and payment status only (no regulated data); mainstream cloud hosting; audit trail on account, order and sync changes.

items.item: Discovery workshops, backlog and acceptance criteria
items.acceptance: Signed-off backlog with acceptance criteria per story, approval rules written down, field ownership per synced entity agreed in principle.

items.item: QuickBooks Online technical spike and data audit of the distributor's company file
items.acceptance: Sandbox app connected over OAuth; written findings on how customers, sub-customers, items, prices, stock and sales tax are held in the real file, and which of them the API exposes.
items.risk_note: +1 day: the real company file's structure is unknown until we see it (sub-customers, price rules, tax setup).

items.item: Architecture and data model design (tenancy, roles, orders, invoices, payments, sync mapping)
items.acceptance: Architecture decision records and an entity diagram reviewed by the team; tenancy and sync-mapping approach agreed.

items.item: User flows and wireframes for the customer portal and the back office
items.acceptance: Clickable wireframes for every screen at desktop and phone widths, reviewed with the distributor.

items.item: Visual design and responsive design system
items.acceptance: Design tokens, component specs and high-fidelity key screens approved by the distributor.

items.item: Repository, CI/CD pipeline, agent instructions and test commands
items.acceptance: A pull request runs lint, type check, unit tests and builds; merges to main deploy to staging automatically.

items.item: Environments and infrastructure as code (dev, staging, production, managed Postgres, secrets, backups)
items.acceptance: Three environments created from code; a restore from backup is tested once.

items.item: Data model and migrations
items.acceptance: Migrations create companies, users, roles, products, prices, orders, lines, invoices, payments, sync mappings and audit tables; seed data loads.

items.item: Audit log, error monitoring and structured logging
items.acceptance: Account, role, order and sync changes write audit entries; errors reach the monitoring tool with request context.

items.item: UI component library and responsive app shell
items.acceptance: Shared components from the design system render at desktop and phone widths in a component catalog.

items.item: Sign-in, password reset and session management
items.acceptance: Users sign in, reset a password and sign out; sessions expire; brute-force attempts are rate-limited.
items.risk_note: +0.5 day: security hardening of the auth flows.

items.item: Company accounts and invitation flow
items.acceptance: A company admin invites a colleague by email with a role; the invite expires; the colleague accepts and lands in the right company.

items.item: Role-based access control and tenant isolation
items.acceptance: Buyer, approver, viewer, company admin and staff permissions enforced in the API and the database queries; an automated test suite proves no endpoint returns another company's data.
items.risk_note: +2 days: cross-tenant leakage tests across every endpoint and role combination; a leak here is the worst failure the portal can have.

items.item: Order approval workflow
items.acceptance: Orders above the company limit wait for an approver, who approves or rejects with a comment; buyer and approver are notified; the decision is audited.
items.risk_note: +2 days: edge cases (limit changed while an order waits, prices change between approval and placement, approver is also the buyer, no approver set, multiple approvers).

items.item: Company admin user management (users, roles, approval limit, deactivation)
items.acceptance: A company admin lists users, changes roles, deactivates a user and sets the approval limit.

items.item: Product catalog with customer prices and stock
items.acceptance: Buyers search and browse synced products and see their price and availability.
items.risk_note: +1 day: customer-specific pricing may need its own price table if QuickBooks price rules are not reachable through the API.

items.item: Cart and checkout
items.acceptance: A buyer builds a cart, adds a PO number and delivery details, and submits; the order goes to approval or is placed according to the limit.

items.item: Order history with search and filters
items.acceptance: Users list their company's orders, filter by date, status and PO, search by product, and open an order to see its lines.

items.item: One-click reorder with change summary
items.acceptance: Reorder fills the cart from a past order at current prices; the cart flags price changes, out-of-stock and discontinued items before submission.
items.risk_note: +1 day: discontinued, inactive and partially available items.

items.item: Email notifications (invites, approvals, order confirmations, payment receipts)
items.acceptance: Each event sends a templated email through the transactional email provider; bounces are logged.

items.item: Invoice list and detail
items.acceptance: Users see open and paid invoices with balances and due dates, and download the invoice PDF.

items.item: Card payment of one or several invoices through Stripe
items.acceptance: A user selects invoices and pays by card in Stripe's hosted payment element; card data never reaches the portal; a receipt is shown and emailed.
items.risk_note: +1 day: invoice balances changing in QuickBooks between selection and payment, and allocation across several invoices.

items.item: Stripe webhooks for payment status
items.acceptance: Signed webhooks update payment status idempotently; replayed and out-of-order events leave the same final state; failures retry.
items.risk_note: +1 day: idempotency, event ordering and failed or disputed payments.

items.item: QuickBooks OAuth connection, token rotation and production app approval
items.acceptance: Staff connect the QuickBooks company from the back office; tokens are stored encrypted and refreshed automatically; an expired connection alerts staff.
items.risk_note: +1 day: Intuit production-key review and refresh-token rotation and expiry handling.

items.item: Sync engine: job queue, change data capture and webhooks, idempotency, rate limits, retries, sync log
items.acceptance: Changes on either side are picked up within minutes; every API write carries an idempotency key; throttling responses back off and retry; every sync action is logged.
items.risk_note: +2 days: QuickBooks throttling and concurrency limits, missed webhooks covered by change-data-capture polling, retry storms.

items.item: Customer mapping and two-way customer sync
items.acceptance: Each portal company links to one QuickBooks customer; contact changes flow both ways; unmatched or duplicate customers are queued for staff.
items.risk_note: +1.5 days: matching existing QuickBooks customers, sub-customers and duplicates.

items.item: Products, prices and stock sync from QuickBooks
items.acceptance: Items, prices and quantities on hand appear in the portal; inactive items are hidden; changes appear within minutes.
items.risk_note: +1.5 days: price rules and customer-specific prices that the API may not expose; inventory quantities only on some QuickBooks plans.

items.item: Portal orders to QuickBooks invoices
items.acceptance: A placed order creates exactly one QuickBooks invoice with the right customer, lines, terms and tax; validation errors are surfaced to staff.
items.risk_note: +1.5 days: sales tax setup (automated sales tax, exemptions), terms and duplicate-prevention on retries.

items.item: Invoices and payments from QuickBooks to the portal
items.acceptance: Invoices, edits, voids, credit memos applied and payments recorded in QuickBooks show in the portal with correct balances.
items.risk_note: +1 day: voided, deleted and edited invoices, and payments applied across several invoices.

items.item: Stripe payments recorded in QuickBooks
items.acceptance: A successful Stripe payment creates one QuickBooks payment applied to the paid invoices, in the agreed deposit account, with fees handled as agreed.
items.risk_note: +1 day: deposit and fee accounting choices and idempotency against webhook replays.

items.item: Conflict detection and staff resolution
items.acceptance: When both sides changed the same record since the last sync, the change is held, staff see a field-level diff and choose which side wins; nothing is overwritten silently.
items.risk_note: +2 days: field-level change tracking against the last synced version, and conflicts on records with dependent lines.

items.item: Reconciliation job and mismatch report
items.acceptance: A nightly job compares customers, open invoices and payments between the portal and QuickBooks and alerts staff to any mismatch.
items.risk_note: +1 day: defining tolerances and handling records created outside the portal.

items.item: Initial data load and customer onboarding
items.acceptance: Customers, products and open invoices load from QuickBooks in a rehearsed dry run; companies link to customers; first admins are invited in batches.
items.risk_note: +1 day: dry runs against a copy of the real company file and cleanup of bad source data.

items.item: Back office shell and staff roles
items.acceptance: Staff sign in to a separate back office area; staff permissions are enforced and audited.

items.item: Manage customer companies and users
items.acceptance: Staff create and edit companies, link them to QuickBooks customers, and manage their users and roles.

items.item: Order administration (view, edit, cancel)
items.acceptance: Staff view and edit orders; an edit to an order already invoiced updates the QuickBooks invoice or raises a conflict.
items.risk_note: +1 day: editing orders that have already become QuickBooks invoices.

items.item: Sync log viewer
items.acceptance: Staff filter the sync log by entity, status and date, and retry a failed sync.

items.item: Payments view
items.acceptance: Staff list payments with status, invoices covered and a link to the Stripe record.

items.item: Integration test suite against the QuickBooks sandbox and Stripe test mode
items.acceptance: Automated end-to-end tests cover order to invoice, payment to QuickBooks, QuickBooks edits to portal and a conflict, and run in CI.
items.risk_note: +1 day: sandbox fixtures and flaky third-party calls.

items.item: Security review and hardening
items.acceptance: Authorization tests, dependency and secret scanning pass; OWASP top-ten review findings fixed; rate limits on public endpoints.

items.item: Performance and load check
items.acceptance: Order history and catalog respond within agreed limits with production-sized data; a load test at peak usage passes.

items.item: Responsive, cross-browser and accessibility pass
items.acceptance: Key flows pass on current desktop and phone browsers and an automated accessibility check; issues fixed.

items.item: User acceptance testing support and feedback rework round
items.acceptance: The distributor's staff and a pilot group of customers test the portal; agreed feedback is fixed and re-verified.

items.item: Release hardening and production cutover
items.acceptance: Production QuickBooks connection and Stripe live keys in place, data loaded, alerts and runbooks ready, rollback rehearsed.

items.item: Documentation and handover
items.acceptance: Architecture notes, runbooks and a staff admin guide delivered and walked through.

items.item: Post-launch hypercare (two weeks)
items.acceptance: Production issues in the first two weeks are triaged and fixed; sync and payment monitoring reviewed daily.

open_questions.question: How does the distributor hold customer-specific prices: QuickBooks price rules, a single list price, or a spreadsheet?
open_questions.affects: Product catalog; products, prices and stock sync; one-click reorder
open_questions.why: QuickBooks price rules may not be reachable through the API; if not, the portal needs its own price table and a way to maintain it.

open_questions.question: Does QuickBooks hold one customer per company, or sub-customers per site or buyer, and how many duplicates exist?
open_questions.affects: Customer mapping and sync; initial data load
open_questions.why: Sub-customers and duplicates need a matching step and a staff review queue before onboarding.

open_questions.question: Which side owns which fields (for example, can staff edit a portal-created invoice in QuickBooks), and who resolves conflicts?
open_questions.affects: Conflict detection and resolution; invoices from QuickBooks; order administration
open_questions.why: Clear field ownership removes most conflicts; open-ended two-way editing makes the conflict module larger.

open_questions.question: How should Stripe payments and fees be booked in QuickBooks (undeposited funds or a clearing account, fee expense, payout reconciliation), and are partial payments or card surcharges allowed?
open_questions.affects: Stripe payments recorded in QuickBooks; reconciliation; card payment
open_questions.why: Payout-level reconciliation and partial payments add mapping and edge cases.

open_questions.question: Does the distributor use QuickBooks automated sales tax, and do customers have exemptions?
open_questions.affects: Portal orders to QuickBooks invoices; cart and checkout
open_questions.why: Tax must be shown at checkout and match the QuickBooks invoice; automated sales tax limits what the API lets us set.

open_questions.question: Where does stock come from (QuickBooks inventory quantities, a warehouse system, or not tracked)?
open_questions.affects: Products, prices and stock sync; one-click reorder; product catalog
open_questions.why: A separate warehouse system is a new integration; no stock tracking removes work.

open_questions.question: Is one approval limit per company enough, or are per-user limits, multi-level approvals or budgets needed?
open_questions.affects: Order approval workflow; company admin user management
open_questions.why: Each extra rule adds states, notifications and tests to the approval workflow.

open_questions.question: Do new orders need a full catalog with search, or is reorder plus quick add by item code enough at launch?
open_questions.why: A quick-add-by-code flow is smaller than a browsable catalog.

assumptions: Responsive web only; no native mobile app.
Payments through Stripe's hosted payment element, so card data never reaches the portal (PCI scope SAQ A).
Sign-in by email and password through a managed auth provider or a mainstream library; no customer SSO.
One QuickBooks Online company (Plus or Advanced) with API access; no other ERP or warehouse system.
Transactional email through a mainstream provider.
Cloud hosting, Stripe fees, auth provider and email provider costs are excluded.
Two weeks of post-launch hypercare are included; ongoing support is not.
